\((f+g)(x) = (3x+5)+(6x-1)\).
Collecting like terms, \((f+g)(x) = 9x+4\).

\((g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))\), so apply \(f\) first and feed its output to \(g\).
\((g \circ f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(3) = 4\).
\((g \circ f)(4) = g(f(4)) = g(6) = 2\).
\((g \circ f)(5) = g(f(5)) = g(2) = 4\).
\(\therefore g \circ f = \{(2,4),(4,2),(5,4)\}\).

\(f\) and \(g\) are inverses of each other when both composites give the identity function.
\((f \circ g)(x) = f(4x+7) = \dfrac{(4x+7)-7}{4} = \dfrac{4x}{4} = x\).
\((g \circ f)(x) = g\left(\dfrac{x-7}{4}\right) = 4\left(\dfrac{x-7}{4}\right)+7 = (x-7)+7 = x\).
Since \((f \circ g)(x) = (g \circ f)(x) = x\) for every real \(x\), \(f\) and \(g\) are inverse functions of each other.

\((f \circ g)(x) = f\left(\sqrt[3]{x-4}\right) = \left(\sqrt[3]{x-4}\right)^{3}+4 = (x-4)+4 = x\).
\((g \circ f)(x) = g(x^{3}+4) = \sqrt[3]{(x^{3}+4)-4} = \sqrt[3]{x^{3}} = x\).
Since \((f \circ g)(x) = (g \circ f)(x) = x\) for every real \(x\), \(f\) and \(g\) are inverse functions of each other.

\((f \circ g)(x) = f\left(\dfrac{2x+3}{x-1}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{2x+3}{x-1}+3}{\dfrac{2x+3}{x-1}-2}\).
Multiplying numerator and denominator by \((x-1)\): \(= \dfrac{(2x+3)+3(x-1)}{(2x+3)-2(x-1)} = \dfrac{5x}{5} = x\).
\((g \circ f)(x) = g\left(\dfrac{x+3}{x-2}\right) = \dfrac{2\left(\dfrac{x+3}{x-2}\right)+3}{\dfrac{x+3}{x-2}-1} = \dfrac{2(x+3)+3(x-2)}{(x+3)-(x-2)} = \dfrac{5x}{5} = x\).
Both composites reduce to the identity (for \(x \ne 1\) and \(x \ne 2\) respectively, where the expressions are defined), hence \(f\) and \(g\) are inverse functions of each other.

An inverse function exists only if \(f\) is one-one and onto.
Here \(f(-1) = 5(-1)^{2} = 5\) and \(f(1) = 5(1)^{2} = 5\), so two different inputs give the same output.
Hence \(f\) is not one-one.
\(\therefore f^{-1}\) does not exist.

\(f(x) = 8\) is a constant function, so every input is sent to \(8\); e.g. \(f(1) = f(2) = 8\).
Hence \(f\) is not one-one (and its range is only \(\{8\}\), so it is not onto \(\mathbb{R}\) either).
\(\therefore f^{-1}\) does not exist.

\(f(x) = \dfrac{6x-7}{3}\) is a non-constant linear function, hence one-one and onto \(\mathbb{R}\); so \(f^{-1}\) exists.
Let \(y = \dfrac{6x-7}{3}\). Then \(3y = 6x-7\), so \(6x = 3y+7\) and \(x = \dfrac{3y+7}{6}\).
Interchanging \(x\) and \(y\), \(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x+7}{6}\).

\(f(x) = \sqrt{4x+5}\) is real only when \(4x+5 \ge 0\), i.e. \(x \ge -\dfrac{5}{4}\), and a square root is never negative, so the range of \(f\) is \([0,\infty)\).
Since the range is not the whole of \(\mathbb{R}\), \(f\) is not onto \(\mathbb{R}\), and an inverse function cannot be defined on \(\mathbb{R}\). (Only after restricting it to \(f : \left[-\dfrac{5}{4},\infty\right) \to [0,\infty)\) does \(f\) become a bijection, the rule of the inverse then being \(\dfrac{x^{2}-5}{4}\).)
\(\therefore f^{-1}\) does not exist.

\(f(x) = 9x^{3}+8\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb{R}\) and takes every real value, so it is one-one and onto; \(f^{-1}\) exists.
Let \(y = 9x^{3}+8\). Then \(9x^{3} = y-8\), so \(x^{3} = \dfrac{y-8}{9}\) and \(x = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{y-8}{9}}\).
Interchanging \(x\) and \(y\), \(f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{x-8}{9}}\).

Test whether \(f\) is one-one across its two branches.
For \(x = -1 < 0\): \(f(-1) = -1+7 = 6\). For \(x = 2 \ge 0\): \(f(2) = 8-2 = 6\).
So \(f(-1) = f(2) = 6\) with \(-1 \ne 2\), i.e. \(f\) is not one-one.
\(\therefore f^{-1}\) does not exist.

Here \(3 > 2\), so the branch \(f(x) = 5x+7\) applies.
\(f(3) = 5(3)+7 = 15+7\).
\(\therefore f(3) = 22\).

Here \(2 \le 2\), so the branch \(f(x) = x^{2}+3\) applies.
\(f(2) = 2^{2}+3 = 4+3\).
\(\therefore f(2) = 7\).

Here \(0 \le 2\), so the branch \(f(x) = x^{2}+3\) applies.
\(f(0) = 0^{2}+3\).
\(\therefore f(0) = 3\).

The middle branch needs \(-3 < x\), which \(x = -3\) does not satisfy; but \(-3 \le -3\), so the branch \(f(x) = 4x-2\) applies.
\(f(-3) = 4(-3)-2 = -12-2\).
\(\therefore f(-3) = -14\).

Here \(-3 < 1 < 3\), so the constant branch applies.
\(\therefore f(1) = 5\).

Here \(5 \ge 3\), so the branch \(f(x) = x^{2}\) applies.
\(f(5) = 5^{2}\).
\(\therefore f(5) = 25\).

\([7.2] = 7\), the greatest integer not exceeding \(7.2\).
\(f(7.2) = 4(7)-3 = 28-3\).
\(\therefore f(7.2) = 25\).

\([0.5] = 0\), the greatest integer not exceeding \(0.5\).
\(f(0.5) = 4(0)-3\).
\(\therefore f(0.5) = -3\).

\(-\dfrac{5}{2} = -2.5\), and the greatest integer not exceeding \(-2.5\) is \(-3\) (not \(-2\), since \(-2 > -2.5\)). So \(\left[-\dfrac{5}{2}\right] = -3\).
\(f\left(-\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = 4(-3)-3 = -12-3\).
\(\therefore f\left(-\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = -15\).

Since \(0 \le \dfrac{1}{4} < 1\), \(\left[\dfrac{1}{4}\right] = 0\) and \(\left\{\dfrac{1}{4}\right\} = \dfrac{1}{4}\).
\(f\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)+5\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{7}{4}\).
\(\therefore f\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = 1.75\).

\(|a| \ge k\) (with \(k>0\)) means \(a \ge k\) or \(a \le -k\). Here \(a = x+4\) and \(k = 5\).
From \(x+4 \ge 5\): \(x \ge 1\).
From \(x+4 \le -5\): \(x \le -9\).
\(\therefore x \in (-\infty,-9] \cup [1,\infty)\).

The moduli change sign at \(x = 2\) and \(x = 4\), so examine the three intervals.
For \(x < 2\): both \(x-4\) and \(x-2\) are negative, so \((4-x)+(2-x) = 3\), i.e. \(6-2x = 3\), giving \(x = 1.5\), which does satisfy \(x < 2\); accepted.
For \(2 \le x \le 4\): \((4-x)+(x-2) = 2\), and \(2 \ne 3\), so there is no solution here.
For \(x > 4\): both are positive, so \((x-4)+(x-2) = 3\), i.e. \(2x-6 = 3\), giving \(x = 4.5\), which does satisfy \(x > 4\); accepted.
Check: at \(x = 1.5\), \(|{-2.5}|+|{-0.5}| = 3\); at \(x = 4.5\), \(|0.5|+|2.5| = 3\).
\(\therefore x = 1.5\) or \(x = 4.5\).

Since \(x^{2} = |x|^{2}\), put \(t = |x|\), where \(t \ge 0\). The equation becomes \(t^{2}+7t+12 = 0\).
\((t+3)(t+4) = 0\), so \(t = -3\) or \(t = -4\).
Both values are negative, whereas \(|x| \ge 0\) for every real \(x\), so neither is admissible.
(Directly: for every real \(x\), \(x^{2}+7|x|+12 \ge 12 > 0\), so the left side can never be \(0\).)
\(\therefore\) there is no real solution; the solution set is \(\{\ \}\).

\(|x| \le k\) (with \(k>0\)) means \(-k \le x \le k\). Here \(k = 3\).
So \(-3 \le x \le 3\).
\(\therefore x \in [-3,3]\).

\(2|x| = 5\) gives \(|x| = \dfrac{5}{2}\).
\(|x| = k\) (with \(k>0\)) means \(x = k\) or \(x = -k\), so \(x = \dfrac{5}{2}\) or \(x = -\dfrac{5}{2}\).
Check: \(2\left|\pm\dfrac{5}{2}\right| = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 5\), so both values satisfy the equation.
\(\therefore x = \pm\dfrac{5}{2}\), i.e. \(x = \pm 2.5\).

solution:
Write \(x = [x]+\{x\}\), where \([x] = n\) is an integer and \(0 \le \{x\} < 1\).
An integer can be pulled out of the greatest-integer bracket, so \([x+[x]] = [n+\{x\}+n] = [2n+\{x\}] = 2n+[\{x\}] = 2n\).
Then \(\big[x+[x+[x]]\big] = [n+\{x\}+2n] = [3n+\{x\}] = 3n\).
So \(3n = 9\), i.e. \([x] = 3\), which holds exactly when \(3 \le x < 4\).
Check with \(x = 3.5\): \([3.5] = 3\), then \([3.5+3] = [6.5] = 6\), then \([3.5+6] = [9.5] = 9\), as required.
\(\therefore x \in [3,4)\), i.e. \(x = 3+r\) where \(0 \le r < 1\).

By definition \(\{x\} = x-[x]\), and this always satisfies \(0 \le \{x\} < 1\).
So \(\{x\}\) is always less than \(1\) and can never exceed \(4\).
\(\therefore\) there is no such \(x\); the solution set is \(\{\ \}\).

\(\{x\} = x-[x]\), so \(\{x\} = 0\) means \(x = [x]\), i.e. \(x\) equals the greatest integer not exceeding it.
That happens precisely when \(x\) is itself an integer, and for every integer \(x\) we do get \(\{x\} = 0\).
\(\therefore x \in \mathbb{Z}\).
_note: The book's key prints "N, Z" for this part. Every natural number is an integer, so the complete solution set is \(\mathbb{Z}\); the answer given here states that. Not counted as a book error, only as a loosely worded key entry.

solution:
\(\{x\} = x-[x] = 0.5\) gives \(x = [x]+0.5\).
Let \([x] = n\), an integer; then \(x = n+0.5\).
Check: for \(x = n+0.5\) we get \([x] = n\) (since \(n \le n+0.5 < n+1\)) and \(\{x\} = 0.5\), as required.
\(\therefore x = n+0.5\), where \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

Write \(x = [x]+\{x\}\). Then \(x+[x] = 2[x]+\{x\}\), so the equation \(2\{x\} = x+[x]\) becomes \(2\{x\} = 2[x]+\{x\}\), i.e. \(\{x\} = 2[x]\).
Now \(0 \le \{x\} < 1\), so \(0 \le 2[x] < 1\), i.e. \(0 \le [x] < \dfrac{1}{2}\).
As \([x]\) is an integer, the only possibility is \([x] = 0\), and then \(\{x\} = 2(0) = 0\), so \(x = [x]+\{x\} = 0\).
Check in the original equation: \(2\{0\} = 0\) and \(0+[0] = 0\), so \(x = 0\) does satisfy it.
\(\therefore x = 0\).
